comments.name: Henry Lieberman
comments.body:
Prof. Bruni,

You don't have to feel guilty for "draining students' transcripts of
meaning". They are already devoid of meaning. And it wasn't your
fault. As a university teacher, your job, like mine, is to help
students learn and develop as thinkers and scholars. You are under no
obligation to act as a screener for companies with lazy HR departments
or hiring managers who want a quick filter, and who can't be bothered
to learn who their applicants really are.

The best way to help students learn is to work with them to
develop their intrinsic love of learning and the subjects you are
teaching. They have to believe you are on their side. The worst thing
about "tough grading" is that it makes students believe that education
is a work-for-grades transaction, and that they are in an adversarial
relationships with you. If they get into a transactional
mindset, then of course they seek to do the least work for the highest
grade.

You have to convince them that *you* care more about getting them
interested and helping them with achievements in the field than in
making them sweat, or judging them. Tough grading undermines that.
You don't have to give As to a flunking student, but be generous with
grades. Treat grades (as the students do) as an externally-imposed
annoyance that you both have to deal with, without letting it consume you. 
Make the classroom interaction be about the learning that
both you and your students are doing, together.

This is a disappointing piece from Mara Gay.  It’s one thing to say that Democratic voters are discontented with the failure to stop Trump’s excesses.  This is correct. But Gay is trying to leverage that into a broader critique of so-called “establishment,” or “conventional” Democrats that is largely wrong.

The argument that the “Establishment,” lost the 2016 and 2024 elections is incredibly  misleading. One big reason we lost in 2016 is that a chunk of progressives sat out the general election under the  fantasy that Clinton wouldn’t be better than Trump.  And 2024 was the result of electing Biden/Harris in 2020. And what Gay is at pains to avoid is that this ticket was chiefly the product of Black voters.  She also doesn’t say that Biden’s strongest support for staying in came from the progressives and that it was the progressives that helped ensure that Harris was the successor (it was “establishment” Pelosi who pushed to get Biden off the ticket and didn’t want to anoint Harris.)

And the reason the progressives stuck with Biden and later Harris is that they liked the Administration’s domestic achievements — which were enacted by all those “establishment” Democrats. 

And as far as Dems handing Trump this victory or that, this is outrageous.  What exactly would a Congresswoman Chevalier done differently had she been there? Gay has nothing to say about this because nothing would have been different. We didn't have the votes.

comments.name: dsws

The quoted poll question conflates open "primaries" with better options such as ranked-choice voting.  

A primary is an election by which a party chooses its nominee.  Open "primaries" are a type of preliminary, not primary,  election.  More importantly, they create bad incentives.  

Suppose there are two parties: the yellow party, preferred by 60% of voters, and the purple party, preferred by 40%.  Suppose further that the purples believe in open participation, while the yellow party values organization and careful vetting. Four purple candidates step up, while the yellows recruit two.  In each party, the votes are split almost evenly.  So each yellow gets about 15% of the vote, and each purple gets about 20%.  The general election features two purples and no yellow, to the frustration of a majority of voters, because the purple party responded correctly to the incentives it faced, while the yellow party didn't.  

A preliminary system forces parties to be control freaks, even if (like the yellows in my example) they would prefer not to be.

comments.name: E
comments.body: There are two separate issues: (1)the process by which a given party chooses who gets to run on its ballot line in the general election=a primary in most cases, but not necessary - some use caucuses or conventions (2)the structure and rules of a general election. (1)is a private matter of political parties. (2)is a matter for the state and the electorate and they should be kept separate. The state could just institute 2-round voting, like they have in multiple countries. The parties could still run whatever process they want to choose a candidate (or two) eligible to run in that general election. If the general electorate has significantly different views from party loyalists, it may be better to produce 2 candidates rather than one for the general, with some discrepancy in their positions. The general election usually proceeds from first to second round by the top 2 or 3 vote getters proceeding to the final round. A ranked choice avoids the multiple rounds by allowing people to express their 2nd, 3rd, etc choice. A lot of the comments here appear to be from dedicated party followers who assume that independents are low information voters. I would ask them to rethink this position as most of the independents I know vote in every election and all were members of some party or other in the past. They are better thought of as disillusioned with both parties, unable to map their heterodox beliefs neatly into either party platform, and more interested in choosing individuals.

Those of us who live directly under the flight path of the regular Uber & Blade helicopter "taxis" in NYC, can testify to the impact of this new mode of travel enjoyed by the uber wealthy. Helicoptering to the World Cup is just an added noise nuisance.  Beginning on Thursday evenings and going through Monday, we have helicopters flying over us, sometimes every two minutes, especially late in the afternoon.  

Because they have to fly low enough not to interfere with the flight paths of JFK and LaGuardia, there are times when they are flying so low that a number of my neighbors are fond of saying that if they got any lower we'd be able to see the passengers picking their noses.    

I live in a three story row house and the noise is deafening.  I feel for my neighbors who live on the top floors of taller apartment buildings. They must feel as if the copters are going to land on their roofs.

That said:   There's nothing like constant helicopter noise to grow sentiment for taxing the wealthy at higher rates.

All can play - rich or poor, male or female, novice or professional, inviting to all races, creeds, and beliefs. The sport welcomes and unites everyone. The 2026 World Cup is just further proof of this.  The ultra-rich can fly in, avoid the crowds, receive rock star treatment, and spend whatever they wish for tickets and access. No matter how much money they have or they spend, it will not buy them an authentic experience or the passion shared by the true fans of this game. The vast majority of fans, whether in the stadiums or in front of a screen do not care about anything other than what is played before them for 90 minutes. Cut away shots of celebrities mean nothing except for the sports organization who paid for many to attend. All in a desperate hope of hobnobbing with those of a similar mind set - being seen with the rich and famous, hoping to fill a void that money cannot buy, but true futbol fans receive for free.

Hamdan is the one suspected of getting support from UAE in money and weapons, turning Darfur into a horror story of bloodletting and ethnic cleansing, Arabized Sudanese against Sudanese of African descent. It is hard to comprehend why UAE would allow its petro-dollars to be used to inflict so much suffering. Consider the contrast: gleaming high towers in Dubai, and poor and displaced people living in tents in Darfur.

comments.body: I have been a caregiver for two people who died of dementia: my stepmother and my husband. Both of them often had episodes of lucidity. It was confusing and upsetting for me as I tried to cope with their decline. Dementia is a personality changer, and not for the better. I have come to believe that the incidents of lucidity were simply random inexplicable events. My stepmother stopped speaking months before she died, but even in her final coma, she seemed to wait for my sister and her daughter to arrive before she died, and then to die after we had left her room. My husband remained verbal until his death. His last words to me, as he rolled up the covers as if he were going on a ride, were: "Now the worries are yours."

He and  I were very close and I wasn't ready to lose him.  Then one morning, when we were "talking" on the phone--I would pretty much do all the talking--he was suddenly his old self again and could remember everything, inquiring after my wife, my young daughter,...  With my wife looking on at me across the kitchen table, I emotionally told him how he had been for the last couple of years and he had no real recollection of it, his response being "That is remarkable."  My wife, who was a veterinarian, cautioned me that this lucidity sometimes happens before people die, and sure enough, he did die soon afterwards. (PMJ)

I similarly found The Old Man and the Sea to be unbearable, and don't get me started on The Grapes of Wrath. 

Mostly I think I was predisposed not to like something I hadn't chosen to read for myself (I did love reading, so it wasn't just petulance at being forced to read at all), but so many years later, thinking back on it, I wonder if we need to revisit our canon of 'Great Books' more frequently. Not that these need to be removed, but the list should be expanded more frequently with newer works that cover a wider range of experiences.

This letter is right that the clock is the real risk but the more urgent question isn't whether AI takes your job, it's whether anyone can catch what an AI system is about to do before it acts.

In December, an Amazon AI coding agent decided the quickest fix to a bug was to delete and rebuild a live production system: 13 hours of outage. Amazon called it a permissions oversight, not a rogue AI but that's the problem.

These systems already make consequential, irreversible decisions faster than the humans supervising them can react. That's not about job displacement; it's about whether AI can be reliably overseen in real time.

NIST scientist Apostol Vassilev published a peer-reviewed proof this year showing no fixed set of safety rules can fully guarantee that (arxiv.org/abs/2512.10100) a mathematical ceiling, not a patchable gap. 

A UC Berkeley benchmark this year found frontier agents pass barely 2.6% of real, economically valuable tasks (arxiv.org/abs/2606.05405)  the capability gap this letter assumes closed isn't close to closed.

And today's AI pricing is subsidised, NOT real cost. 

Uber ran that playbook: price below cost until the taxi trade broke, & by the time the true cost was visible, the industry was gone +much of that workforce landed in precarious gig work instead.

It’s as if we built powerful machines freeing us from backbreaking work, but the only way to turn on those powerful machines is by being as fit as an Olympic athlete!

Imagine if a bulldozer could only be turned on via a crankshaft that required the driver to exert a force comparable to bench pressing 200 pounds!

If this paradox happened with machines, everyone would need to go to the gym to build the strength required to turn on their car or their laptop!

So, will humans need to go to “brain gyms” in order to be savvy enough to interact well with A.I.?

Or will A.I. continue to improve to the point that human oversight and feedback will be unnecessary?

In my experience creating A.I. prompts, my conclusion is that—in the near term, at least--humans will need to up their mental game! Those who don’t will allow A.I. to do many foolish things.

The procedures to treat them involve injecting superglue into bad/closed vein, or radiofrequency or laser ablation (they are eventually  absorbed by the body). These are the top two ways now; stripping - removing the vein- is not a preferred method of treatment currently.
None of this addresses the issues of bad valves in one's veins, so more varicose veins are likely in future. How to lessen future issues?  The genetics of whether one is prone to this and/or hormonal changes are out of one's hands, but the things people can control: wear compression stockings always, elevate legs often; lose weight; no smoking. Move often- sitting for long spells is the worst. Exercise regularly, especially to build calf muscles to help pump blood back up the leg.

I decided to travel to Parintins to show a different side of Brazilian popular culture, going beyond the Carnival celebrations the country is known for. I had heard that the bull, and the rivalry over it, was central to Amazonian identity, and I wanted to see it up close to understand what it meant to people there.

What I found was that this tradition had a lot to do with people’s desire to preserve their complex history, which mixes Indigenous and Afro-Brazilian folklore with traditions brought over by colonial settlers. While reporting in Parintins, I was also struck by how, despite people’s impassioned allegiances, the rivalry was mostly civil and respectful. This stood out to me, given how polarized Brazil is right now in other realms like politics and ideology.
